title: Private CP — Surge Scaling & Rollback Playbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This playbook is an operator-facing tactical guide for handling short-term surge scaling, controlled capacity rotations, and clean rollback during Private Control Plane (VPC / on-prem) operations. It is intentionally concise and pragmatic — aimed at runbook execution during incidents and planned surges.

Audience:
- Field operators and SREs responsible for customer private control plane provisioning and on-call rotations.
- Solutions engineers executing customer cutovers and scale tests.

When to use:
- Traffic or API request rate surges that exhaust reserved GPU or control-plane proxies.
- Planned customer load tests or migration windows requiring burst capacity.
- Failed automated scaling or when an upgrade causes regressions and a rollback is required.

Assumptions / prerequisites:
- You have active access to the customer VPC account or on-prem admin console and the private control plane bastion.
- Terraform state for the private control plane is in the customer-owned backend defined in terraform.tfstate (S3/GCS) and you have the locking credentials.
- KMS keys and HSM/KMS roles are available and not blocked by policy.
- Certificate issuer (internal CA or Vault) reachable from management host.
- Slack incident channel and runbook owner assigned.

Quick glossary:
- CP: control plane (the Private Control Plane components: api-server, configstore, router, autoscaler, metrics-collector)
- Worker pool / GPU pool: nodes backing model-serving; often managed by kube or custom node-pool controller.
- Rotation: evict-and-drain pattern used to stage updates across nodes without dropping traffic.

Signal detection (when to trigger this runbook):
- Latency SLO breaches > 10% above baseline for 3 consecutive 1m windows
- Error rate > 2% for user-facing endpoints or > 5% for internal control plane apis
- GPU utilization > 85% sustained for 5m across primary pool or queue length growth > 50%
- Terraform apply failed to converge for model-serving autoscaler resources

High-level flow:
1) Triage & impact scoping
2) If surge: execute safe burst (hot add) procedure
3) If instability or failed autoscale: run controlled rotation or rollback to prior known-good Terraform state
4) Verify, stabilize, and follow up with incident ticket and postmortem notes

1) Triage & impact scoping
- Immediately set incident channel and @oncall. Capture: customer name, control plane id, region, current terraform workspace, link to state backend.
- Run: terraform workspace show (confirm workspace), and query state storage (aws s3 ls <state key> or gcloud storage objects list).
- Note last successful apply: GH PR / tag in linked_artifacts or terraform remote state meta.
- Confirm whether a recent deploy/upgrade coincides with the onset of issues.

2) Safe burst (hot add) for capacity surges (non-destructive)
Goal: add temporary capacity without changing control-plane code paths or performing rolling restarts.
Prereqs: hot-burst policy allowed in customer contract and autoscaler override credentials available.
Steps:
- On infra bastion, export customer AWS/GCP creds and kubeconfig for the target cluster.
- Increase worker pool size via cloud console or Terraform short-circuit: run a temporary override script that calls provider APIs directly (recommended) rather than terraform apply to avoid state drift. Example (AWS autoscaling group): aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name <asg> --desired-capacity <N+X> --honor-cooldown
- If the infra uses a managed nodepool (GKE/AKS/EKS), prefer provider API scaling to avoid long terraform plans.
- Wait for nodes to register (kubectl get nodes --watch). Confirm scheduling with kubectl get pods -o wide and that critical pods are balanced across new nodes.
- Monitor latency/error metrics and token throughput. If stable after 10–15 minutes, update incident channel and note temporary capacity increase.
- Commit a short-lived terraform change if desired (state-only change) to reflect the temporary size: create a plan but do NOT apply unless long-term change required.

3) Controlled rotation (evict-and-drain) when autoscaler is unstable or after a rolling upgrade
Goal: rotate nodes or control-plane instances in small batches to minimize disruption.
Principles:
- Max parallel rotation = 1/10th of total pool or 2 nodes, whichever is smaller
- Verify readiness probes and canary endpoints before proceeding to the next batch
Procedure:
- Identify rotation candidate set (by age, kernel version, or failed readiness checks).
- For each node in the batch:
  - cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>
  - drain with timeout: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=300s
  - monitor pod rescheduling and API latency; wait for system and model-serving pods to be Ready
  - if pods fail to reschedule, uncordon and abort rotation; escalate to SRE lead
- If using upstream kube, ensure PV mounts remount correctly and that any local caches are warmed before taking next node
- After batch completes, run smoke tests against a small set of user prompts and run evals (script path referenced below)

4) Rollback plan (Terraform state and image rollback)
When to rollback:
- Client-facing regressions that cannot be mitigated by scaling or rotation
- New control-plane or sidecar image introduces errors across multiple nodes
Rollback steps (fast path):
- Confirm the last known-good terraform state snapshot id from state backend (S3/GCS object version or state-lock record)
- If the change was only an image bump, prepare to redeploy previous image tag via kubectl set image or Helm rollback; prefer this for speed
- For Terraform rollbacks that change infra primitives (ASG sizes, subnet mappings):
  - Lock the state: terraform force-unlock if stale lock and ensure team aware
  - Create a plan that targets only the resources that must be reverted (avoid large diffs)
  - Apply with --target restrictions (terraform apply -target=module.pool -auto-approve) to minimize blast radius
- If state is inconsistent or apply fails, escalate to infra lead and consider reprovisioning a fresh cluster and performing blue-green traffic cutover to minimize customer downtime

5) Verification checklist (post action)
- System health: all control-plane pods Ready and stable for 10m
- Observability: no tailing errors in router logs, metrics back to baseline, token cost metrics normalized
- Customer reports: confirm with SE/CS that customer-side traffic is healthy
- Update incident with exact terraform commands used, node ids, and timestamps

Post-incident steps and follow-up:
- Open a short postmortem draft in Confluence with timeline, root cause hypothesis, and recommended durable fixes (e.g., autoscaler tuning, smaller default batch rotation sizes, increases in reserved capacity)
- Add a regression test to the private cp e2e suite that reproduces the surge pattern if feasible
- If rollback was used, schedule a controlled re-attempt of the upgrade in a canary customer environment with load replay

Useful commands and snippets (examples)
- Show workspace: terraform workspace show
- Lock state (S3): aws s3api get-object --bucket <state-bucket> --key <key> --version-id <version>
- Temporarily scale ASG (AWS): aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name my-pool-asg --desired-capacity 10 --honor-cooldown
- Quick image rollback (kubectl): kubectl -n redwood set image deployment/router router=redwood/router:2025-01-12-rc1
- Drain node: kubectl drain ip-10-0-2-34.ec2.internal --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=300s

Known gotchas and troubleshooting notes:
- Terraform drift: if providers were changed manually (hot add via API), terraform plan may show unexpected diffs. Document any manual API calls in the incident ticket and plan a state reconciliation window.
- KMS access errors: rotation/upgrade often fails when KMS IAM roles lack kms:Encrypt permissions in target account. Confirm role bindings before any state-changing operation.
- Long PVC attach times on older on-prem nodes: allow longer drain timeouts and stagger batch sizes
- Pod affinity: large stateful pods with strict anti-affinity can block rotation; plan special case handling for those workloads

Appendix: quick reference links and scripts
- smoke test script: gs://private-cp-scripts/smoke/smoke-test.sh (run from management bastion)
- load replay tool: GH: redwood/load-replay (branch: private-cp-replays)
- Terraform module for scaling overrides: GH: redwood/infra-terraform-private-cp/modules/scale-override

Contact matrix:
- On-call SRE: @oncall-private-cp (PagerDuty)
- Private CP eng lead: Marta Ruiz (mruiz@redwood.ai)
- Solutions escalation: Connor Blake (cblake@redwood.ai)

Decision log (short):
- 2025-01-10: Adopted batch size limit of max(2, floor(pool/10)) after two customer incidents where larger batches caused cascading OOMs
- 2025-02-20: Added "hot add via provider API" as an approved temporary mitigation to reduce Terraform plan-induced delays

Notes-to-self / TODOs:
- Add a dedicated terraform state-reconciliation guide with examples of converting manual API changes into state updates (low priority)
- Add KMS role verification into the pre-cutover checklist
